title: What backtesting app do you actually trust once the strategy gets more complicated?
author: GD2000GD
selftext:
I have tried a few backtesting apps and keep running into the same trade-off.



The easier platforms are fine until I want to define the entry and exit more precisely, change the position sizing, include realistic costs, or compare several versions without losing track of what I changed.



Then the more advanced platforms can do almost anything, but every small trading idea turns into another Python project.



I am not looking for an AI that gives me a “winning strategy” or shows me the prettiest equity curve. I mainly want something for US stocks where I can build or describe the rules, understand what was actually tested, compare different versions, and ideally move the same logic into paper trading without rebuilding everything.



I can read some code, but I do not want to spend more time setting up infrastructure than testing the idea itself



What are you currently using, and what does it genuinely do well?



More importantly, where does it start to break for you? Please do not just drop the name of an app. I would rather hear “good for this, bad for that.”

comments.author: Accomplished_Netchee
comments.body: There really is no single best one imo. QuantConnect is the deepest if you want full control over the research, code, data, backtest and eventual deployment, but the learning curve is real even with Mia helping. VIBTRA is almost the opposite experience: describe the strategy, review the generated logic, keep the different runs separate and move the same idea into paper trading. Composer is good if you prefer building rule-based systems visually and want backtesting plus execution in one place. TrendSpider makes the most sense when your ideas begin with charts, indicators and technical conditions because the tester, AI models and bots are built around that workflow. They all solve a different version of the problem, so it depends on whether you value control, speed, automation or visual research most.

comments.author: DiamondHandzzz2x
comments.body: If you can tolerate Python, vectorbt is still hard to beat for research. It works directly with pandas and NumPy objects and is built for testing large numbers of variations quickly. You get much more control over the data and analysis, but obviously you are back to writing the logic yourself and building the surrounding workflow. It is a library, not the polished app experience you seem to be asking for.

comments.author: Rare_Inflation3178
comments.body:
This is the exact gap I keep seeing. Easy tools break once the logic gets custom, and flexible tools turn every idea into a software project.  
For me the missing piece is reproducibility: versioned strategy logic, consistent cost assumptions, and moving the same strategy into paper trading without rewriting it.  
These days, I’ve been trying a tool that’s aiming to solve a very similar problem.

comments.author: RemoraEdge
comments.body:
Backtesting app? I’m assuming you mean a strategy analyzer that tests out your automated strategy over historical data?

Why don’t you want AI to use python for this? It will be much faster and more customizable - allow you to compare different versions like you said. It’ll be a lot faster than using a proprietary analyzer.

comments.author: Quant-Builder
comments.body:
I know of one.   
US Equities only. No options. And you actually trade the stocks. It's set up so you can trade them in a few clicks.   
  
How it works: you build your quant models, using the inputs you normally use, anything from momentum to trend to fundamentals and macro like PE, oil prices or cpi.  
You train, backtest and refine the model. Then you can track the model. Have it auto-score every night, generate new picks and follow along. Then anytime you want, you can just select all the picks it has every morning and trade them. You put the exits. Stop Loss, trail stop loss, profit taking, or just sell on model target end date if no exits hit. (5 days for example)

FYI, this isn't algo trading where you just have the bot trade. You make the decisions every morning. You can build various models for various scenarios (long discretionary, short tech) and you make the trade. I can give you the link if this sound interesting to you

comments.author: LouZEverything
comments.body:
A backtest usually misses all the fun little realities that show up the second you trade live. Oh yeah, slippage is basically non-existent in backtest fantasyland. You click buy, and magically the market gives you the exact price you wanted, like it’s your personal assistant. The bid and ask spread apparently behaves like a well-trained golden retriever in backtests. In real life, the spread can widen right when you need it not to, because of course it does. Backtests love to pretend your entire order got filled perfectly, instantly, and without drama. Real markets are more like, “Here’s half your order filled at a weird price. Good luck.” In backtest world, you are always first in line. No waiting, no competition, no one ahead of you. Just straight VIP treatment from the market, which is adorable. A backtest looks at the candle after all the chaos is over and acts like it knew what happened. Live trading is watching that candle throw a tantrum in real time.  
Your backtest engine says, “Great trade.” Your broker says, “Interesting theory.” And somehow both are using different versions of reality. Backtests never hesitate, panic, revenge trade, move stops too early, or stare at a setup and suddenly forget the whole plan. Must be nice.  
The chart looks brilliant after the fact. The signal is sitting there like, “Obviously you should’ve entered here.” Meanwhile live, it showed up three bars late wearing sunglasses and pretending it was there the whole time. Backtests assume liquidity is just always available, like the market has an unlimited snack drawer. Real life says, “Cute order. Let’s see who actually wants to fill it.”  Backtests treat news like a calm little calendar event. Live markets treat news like someone kicked open the door and threw a chair across the room. A strategy can look amazing historically, then suddenly stop working live like it went on vacation and forgot to tell you. Bottom line, backtesting is useful, but it is not reality. If you want to test the logic it’s excellent but for testing live profitability not so much.

comments.author: LankyAwareness2258
comments.body: Honestly the wall you're hitting isn't the app, it's state. A simple entry/exit backtest is basically stateless — check a condition, fire a signal. Once you add partial exits, trailing logic, or multi-timeframe confirmation, you're really building a state machine on top of whatever framework you picked, and that's where "flexible" tools turn into spaghetti. The other quiet killer: any indicator that references a not-yet-closed bar looks perfect on the historical run and falls apart live — worth auditing exactly what bar-close each input was calculated on, not just the date range you tested. Less an app problem, more a "did you design the state machine or are you bolting conditions onto a linear script" problem.
